body.en: A *constructor* is a member with the same name as its class and no return type (not even void). It is called automatically when an object is created with new, and it initialises the instance variables. If a class has no constructor, Java supplies a default constructor that sets numbers to 0, booleans to false and references to null. A parameterised constructor takes arguments: new Student("Asha", 12). Constructors can be overloaded like methods.

body.en: Inside an instance method or constructor, this is a reference to the current object, the object on which the method was called. It is used to tell a field from a parameter with the same name (this.roll = roll), to pass the current object to another method, and to call another constructor of the same class from the first line of a constructor: this(0, "unknown"). Static methods have no this, because they are not called on an object.

this(...) calls another constructor (first line only)

tagline.en: Why a method cannot change a caller's int but can change the contents of a caller's array, static versus instance members, the this keyword, and method overloading.

myth.en: Arrays are passed by reference, so if a method does arr = new int[5]; the caller's array is replaced too.

truth.en: The method has only a copy of the reference. Changing an element (arr[0] = ...) changes the shared object, but making the parameter point to a new object (arr = new ...) changes only the local copy. "Pass by reference" sounds as if the caller's variable itself is handed over. In Java only its value (the address) is copied, so re-pointing the copy cannot move the caller's variable.

say.en: Java copies every argument. A primitive copy cannot affect the caller; a reference copy reaches the same object.
Changing an object's contents through a parameter is seen by the caller; re-pointing the parameter is not.
A static variable has one copy per class; instance variables have one copy per object. Static methods cannot use this.
this refers to the current object and resolves name clashes between parameters and instance variables.
Overloaded methods share a name but differ in their parameter lists; a different return type alone is not enough.
